question: What does the Bible say about whether salvation can be lost?
intro: Christians ask whether a person who has been saved can lose that salvation, and they read the New Testament as holding promises that those who are Christ's are kept beside warnings that some turn away and are cut off. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them. The passages come from several New Testament writers, and readers differ on whether they hold one view or speak to different situations.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that salvation is God's gift, that Christ will not drive away the one who comes to him, that believers are urged to continue in the faith, and that some people abandon the faith. The readings differ on whether a person who has been saved can lose that salvation, and on who the warning passages address.

passages.quote: For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God,
the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.
strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith.
in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons,

readings.label: Falling away is possible: the warnings address people who have been saved, and the one who remains in Christ is kept
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the warnings of Hebrews, John 15 and the letters of Paul to be addressed to people who have received salvation, and take them to mean that a person who has been saved can turn away and be lost, and that the one who remains in Christ is kept. Catholic teaching holds that the life of grace is lost by what is called mortal sin and is restored through repentance (Catechism 1855-1861; Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 14); it also holds that faith can remain after grace is lost by mortal sin, and urges firm hope in God's help while denying certainty of final perseverance (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapters 13 and 15). Eastern Orthodox readers speak of a freedom to turn from God that stays with a person through life, and of salvation as a way walked to its end; the Confession of Dositheus (1672) holds that a baptized person who falls is restored through repentance and the Church's penance. Wesleyan and Methodist readers hold that a believer who turns from Christ can fall from grace and can return: the Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church (Article XII) say that repentance is not to be denied to those who sin after justification, and the Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion among its doctrinal standards, and the United Methodist Confession of Faith (Article IX) says that it is possible to depart from grace and fall into sin; Wesley's sermon A Call to Backsliders teaches that those who have fallen from grace can be restored. The Assemblies of God states this reading in its bylaws and position paper (salvation may be abandoned by willfully turning from Christ, while the believer is secure in a living relationship with him), and members of Pentecostal churches of the Wesleyan holiness line share it. The National Association of Free Will Baptists says in its Treatise (chapter XIII) that the truly regenerate are in danger of falling and are to watch and pray lest they be lost; General Baptist readers hold this reading, and differ from the Baptist readers below on whether a believer can fall away. Lutheran teaching holds that a believer can fall from faith (the Formula of Concord, Epitome IV, rejects the teaching that faith and the Holy Spirit are not lost by wilful sin), that God keeps believers in faith through his word and sacraments, and that a person who has fallen away is brought back by the word of forgiveness (Augsburg Confession XII); Lutheran readers take assurance to rest on the promise of that word, and differ from Reformed readers on whether those who believe can fall away. Anabaptist readers hold that the warnings are addressed to the gathered church of believers: the Dordrecht Confession (1632, Article XVI) speaks of a church member who sins unto death and so forfeits the kingdom of God, the 1995 Mennonite confession (Article 14) treats church discipline as a sign of God's offer of forgiveness to believers who drift from faithful discipleship, and the same confession holds faith and faithful obedience to be inseparable (Article 8). The Church of England's Article XVI holds that after receiving the Holy Spirit a person may depart from grace given and, by God's grace, rise again; Anglican members differ on how far that stands beside Article XVII.

passages.quote: and then have fallen away-to be restored to repentance, because they themselves are crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.
passages.note: Read as describing people who have shared in the Spirit and the gifts of God and then fallen away. Hebrews 6:4 describes them: "It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, who have shared in the Holy Spirit,"
passages.context_note: The sentence opens in 6:4: 'It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened'. After the picture of the land in 6:7-8, the passage turns in 6:9: 'Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case-things that accompany salvation.'

passages.quote: If we deliberately go on sinning after we have received the knowledge of the truth, no further sacrifice for sins remains
passages.note: Read as addressed to the author's own readers, who are included in the "we".

passages.quote: If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned.
passages.note: A branch in Christ that does not remain.

passages.quote: You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ; you have fallen away from grace.
passages.note: Read as addressing believers who have fallen away from grace.

passages.quote: if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off.
passages.note: Read as a warning to the Gentile believers that they too will be cut off if they do not continue.

passages.quote: continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling.
passages.note: Believers told to continue working out their own salvation with fear and trembling.

passages.quote: If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first.
passages.note: Read as describing people who knew the Lord and returned to the corruption.

passages.quote: if a righteous man turns from his righteousness and practices iniquity, committing the same abominations as the wicked, will he live? None of the righteous acts he did will be remembered. Because of the unfaithfulness and sin he has committed, he will die.
passages.note: Read for the chapter's principle that each person answers for his own turning. The same chapter says: "But if a wicked man turns from the wickedness he has committed and does what is just and right, he will save his life." (Ezekiel 18:27)

passages.quote: some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith
passages.note: Paul urges Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience, which, he says, some have rejected and so have shipwrecked their faith.

passages.quote: none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God
passages.note: The writer warns the brothers that a heart of unbelief can turn away from the living God.

passages.quote: the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall
passages.note: Paul warns those who think they stand firm to take care not to fall, after reviewing Israel's wilderness failures.

passages.quote: I myself will not be disqualified
passages.note: Paul disciplines his body so that after preaching to others he will not himself be disqualified.

passages.quote: if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him
passages.note: God says his righteous one will live by faith, and that he takes no pleasure in one who shrinks back.

passages.quote: They believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away
passages.note: In the parable of the sower, those on rocky ground receive the word with joy but have no root and fall away under testing.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take John 10:27-29 to speak of the sheep who listen to Christ and follow him, with no one able to snatch them from his hand, and take Romans 8:38-39 to list powers outside the believer without naming the believer's own turning. They take John 6:39 and Philippians 1:6 as promises of God's faithfulness to those who remain in him. They take 1 John 2:19 to describe people who had been in the community and left. They take Hebrews 6:9 and 10:39 as the author's confidence about the readers within a letter that warns those same readers. They take Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30 to name the Spirit's seal on those who have heard and believed, and read the command in 4:30 not to grieve the Spirit as one given to believers, as the warnings are. They take Hebrews 7:25, John 17:11, Luke 22:32 and Jude 24 as Christ's intercession and God's keeping of those who continue in him.

readings.label: The perseverance of the saints (the Calvinist, or Reformed, reading): God keeps those he has saved to the end, and the warnings are among the means he uses to keep them
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to teach that those God has saved are kept in faith to the end, so that a person who is truly in Christ will persevere and will not be lost, and that the warnings are the means by which God keeps his people in faith. Reformed teaching, often called Calvinist, states this as the perseverance of the saints and joins it to its account of election. The Westminster Confession (chapter 17), the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, and the Canons of Dort (Fifth Head), held by the Christian Reformed Church, add that a true believer can fall into grievous sin and lose the comfort of assurance for a time, but not totally or finally (Westminster Confession 17.1-3; Canons of Dort, Fifth Head, Articles 4-7), and the Canons name the gospel's warnings among the means God uses to preserve his people (Article 14). Baptist confessions state it: Southern Baptists in the Baptist Faith and Message 2000 (Article V) and Baptists of the 1689 London Confession (chapter 17). The Church of England's Article XVII speaks of those whom God has chosen in Christ as brought by him to everlasting salvation, and Anglican members differ among themselves. Its holders speak of people who leave the faith as people whose faith was not the saving kind, and not as saved people who lost their salvation, and they hold the warnings to be real and to be heeded by every believer. Assurance in this reading rests on God's promise and is confirmed by the fruit of continuing faith.

passages.quote: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand.
passages.note: Eternal life given, with no one able to take the sheep from Christ's hand.

passages.quote: For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.
passages.note: Read with 2:12 as working out salvation while God works in the believer.

passages.quote: And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.
passages.note: Read as a chain in which no one called is dropped before glorification.

passages.quote: neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
passages.note: Nothing in all creation separates believers from God's love.

passages.quote: He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus.
passages.note: God completes the work he begins.

passages.quote: who through faith are shielded by God's power for the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time.
passages.note: Believers shielded by God's power, through faith, for a salvation yet to come.

passages.quote: They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us.
passages.note: Read as saying that those who leave were not among those who truly belonged.

passages.quote: I will make an everlasting covenant with them: I will never turn away from doing good to them, and I will put My fear in their hearts, so that they will never turn away from Me.
passages.note: A promise to Israel and Judah in its own chapter. Reformed holders cite it as God's everlasting covenant with his people, and that is their reading.

passages.quote: do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption
passages.note: Paul tells believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom they were sealed for the day of redemption.

passages.quote: having heard and believed the word of truth-the gospel of your salvation-you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit
passages.note: Paul says that when the Ephesians heard and believed the gospel they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

passages.quote: He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them
passages.note: Christ is able to save completely those who come to God through him, because he always lives to intercede for them.

passages.quote: Holy Father, protect them by Your name
passages.note: In his prayer before the cross, Jesus asks the Father to protect his disciples by the Father's name.

passages.quote: I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail
passages.note: Jesus tells Simon he has prayed that his faith will not fail, and that after turning back he is to strengthen his brothers.

passages.quote: Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence
passages.note: Jude's closing praise names God as the one able to keep believers from stumbling and present them unblemished.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29 as warnings to a congregation that includes people who have shared in its gifts and privileges without trusting Christ, and as the means God uses to keep his own, with Hebrews 6:9 and 10:39 stating the author's confidence about the readers. They take John 15:2 and 15:6 to speak of branches joined outwardly to Christ that bear no fruit, Colossians 1:23 and Hebrews 3:14 to name continuing in faith as the mark of those who belong, and Galatians 5:4 to describe the person who turns to the law as the ground of acceptance. They take 2 Peter 2:20-21 to speak of false teachers, and Ezekiel 18:24 to speak of life in Israel's covenant, with Jeremiah 32:40 naming what God promises in the new one. They take Luke 8:13 to describe a faith that had no root, 1 Timothy 1:19 to speak of people such as Hymenaeus and Alexander (1:20), 1 Corinthians 9:27 and 10:12 and Hebrews 3:12 as warnings that God uses to keep his own, and Hebrews 10:38 with the author's confidence in 10:39: "But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls."

readings.label: Eternal security: eternal life is given when a person believes and rests on Christ's work and God's faithfulness, so it is not lost
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to say that eternal life is given when a person believes and is a present possession, held by what Christ has done and by God's faithfulness. The General Association of Regular Baptist Churches states the security of the saints in Article XIII of its Articles of Faith (all who are truly born again are kept by God the Father for Jesus Christ), and many Baptist and free-church readers state this as the security of the believer. Many of its holders use the phrase “once saved, always saved” for it; that is the popular form, and the phrase is not in the Baptist Faith and Message or the 1689 London Confession, which state the second reading. Some independent Charismatic churches hold it; the Assemblies of God disapproves of it by bylaw. Holders of this reading differ among themselves on whether every believer will keep believing and on what the warning passages address. Some say that a believer who lives in sin is disciplined by God and loses reward, not salvation.

passages.quote: For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.
passages.note: Eternal life promised to everyone who believes.

passages.quote: whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.
passages.note: Eternal life stated as a present possession, with no coming under judgment.

passages.quote: Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
passages.note: No condemnation for those in Christ, stated in the present.

passages.quote: who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God's possession, to the praise of His glory.
passages.note: Read as naming the Spirit as the pledge of the inheritance until the redemption.

passages.quote: If it is burned up, he will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.
passages.note: Loss of the work done, with the person still saved.

passages.quote: if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.
passages.note: God's faithfulness stated as holding when ours fails.

passages.quote: because by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified.
passages.note: A single offering with a completed result for all time.

passages.quote: I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.
passages.note: Believers told they may know that they have eternal life.

passages.quote: I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand
passages.note: Jesus says he gives his sheep eternal life, that they will never perish, and that no one can snatch them from his hand.

passages.quote: neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities
passages.note: Paul lists powers that, he is convinced, cannot separate believers from the love of God in Christ; the list runs on into verse 39.

passages.quote: those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified
passages.note: Paul's chain: those God predestined he called, those he called he justified, and those he justified he glorified.

passages.quote: you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit
passages.note: Paul says that when the Ephesians heard and believed the gospel they were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.

passages.quote: in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption
passages.note: Paul says believers were sealed by the Holy Spirit for the day of redemption.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading differ among themselves about the warning passages. Some take Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29 to speak of the discipline of God's people and of loss of reward, as in 1 Corinthians 3:15, and not of loss of eternal life; others take them as the second reading does, as warnings that describe people who professed faith. They take John 15:6 to speak of the loss of a fruitless branch's place and Galatians 5:4 to describe a person turning to the law as the way to live. They take Colossians 1:23, Romans 11:22 and Matthew 24:13 to name what marks a genuine faith, or to address groups of people, and not to state a condition on which eternal life is held. They take Ezekiel 18:24 to speak to Israel in its own covenant.

terms.note: The Reformed term for the teaching that those whom God has saved are kept in faith to the end and will not finally fall away.

The term used by many Baptist and free-church readers, and in popular use, for the teaching that a person who has been saved cannot lose that salvation; its holders differ on whether every believer will continue in faith.
Turning away from the faith after having professed or received it; the traditions differ on whether it can happen to a person who has been saved, or whether it shows that the person was not saved.
The Catholic term for a grave sin freely chosen that breaks the life of grace in a person; it is restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance.
A phrase taken from Galatians 5:4; Wesleyan readers use it for a believer who has turned from Christ, and others take the verse to speak of turning to the law.

A believer's confidence in his or her own salvation; traditions differ on what it rests on: the promise of God, the fruit of a continuing faith, the witness of the Spirit, or the sacraments. The Catholic teaching is that no one may hold with the certainty of faith that he will persevere to the end, apart from a special revelation.
The Eastern Orthodox term for the human will cooperating with God's grace through life.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, chapters 13 to 15 and canons 16, 23, 27 and 28
further_reading.says: It teaches that no one may claim with certainty that he will persevere to the end and that hope rests on God's help, that those who lose justifying grace are restored through the sacrament of penance, and that grace is lost by any mortal sin while faith itself may remain.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1854-1864 (Mortal and Venial Sin)
further_reading.says: It teaches that mortal sin destroys charity and sanctifying grace, that unrepented it excludes a person from Christ's kingdom, and that it calls for a new initiative of God's mercy, normally in the sacrament of reconciliation (1855-1861).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decrees 14 and 16
further_reading.says: Decree 14 holds that the regenerate still need grace for any work worthy of a Christian life and can choose whether to cooperate with it, and Decree 16 says that a baptized person who falls into sin or apostasy and returns receives again, through penance, the adoption of a son which he had lost.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 269, 305, 306 and 384
further_reading.says: It teaches that those who sin after baptism are more guilty than the unbaptized but can obtain pardon through penitence, that the impenitent are cut off from the Church, and that God does not will sinners to perish: they perish by their own choice.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article XII (Of Repentance)
further_reading.says: It teaches that those who fall into sin after baptism receive forgiveness whenever they turn back, and condemns those who deny that the justified can lose the Holy Spirit and those who refuse absolution to the repentant.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Article IV (Good Works), paragraph 19
further_reading.says: It rejects the teaching that faith and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit are not lost by wilful sin.

further_reading.title: Formula of Concord, Epitome, Article XI (Election), affirmative theses 7 to 12
further_reading.says: It teaches that Christ promises the Holy Spirit's help to persevere to eternal salvation, that believers are to look for their election in Christ and the Gospel and are told that no one can snatch them from his hand, and that those who are not saved refuse or disregard God's Word.

further_reading.title: Luther's Large Catechism, Holy Baptism, paragraphs 77 to 82
further_reading.says: It teaches that baptism stands even if a person falls into sin, so that access to it remains, and that repentance is a return and approach to baptism.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 17 (Of the Perseverance of the Saints)
further_reading.says: It teaches that those accepted in Christ and sanctified by the Spirit cannot fall away totally or finally, that this rests on God's decree and Christ's intercession and not on the believer's own will, and that believers may fall into grievous sins and lose some grace and comfort for a time.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, question 36
further_reading.says: It lists perseverance in grace to the end among the benefits that accompany or flow from justification, adoption and sanctification.

further_reading.title: Canons of Dort, Fifth Main Point of Doctrine (Perseverance of the Saints), Articles 3 to 7 and 14
further_reading.says: It teaches that God preserves believers to the end, that through their own fault they can fall into serious sins and lose the sense of grace for a time, that God does not withdraw the Holy Spirit completely nor let them lose adoption or justification, and that he preserves them through the gospel with its warnings and calls to obey.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 1, 53 and 54
further_reading.says: It teaches that Christ watches over the believer so that not a hair can fall from the head, that the Holy Spirit will remain with the believer forever, and that the believer always will be a living member of the community Christ preserves.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, chapter 24 (Election Confirmed by the Calling of God), sections 6 to 10
further_reading.says: Calvin teaches that Christ keeps those the Father has given him and none of the elect will perish, and that those who seem to fall away never clung to Christ with the heartfelt confidence that establishes election.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Articles XVI (Of Sin after Baptism) and XVII (Of Predestination and Election)
further_reading.says: Article XVI says that after receiving the Holy Spirit we may depart from grace given and fall into sin, and by God's grace rise again, and Article XVII says that those God chose in Christ he decreed to deliver from curse and damnation and bring to everlasting salvation.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Article XII (Of Sin After Justification)
further_reading.says: It teaches that not every sin willingly committed after justification is the sin against the Holy Spirit, and that repentance is not to be denied to those who sin after justification and turn back to God.

further_reading.title: Global Methodist Church, Doctrinal Standards: the Articles of Religion and the Confession of Faith
further_reading.says: The Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion and the Confession of Faith as its doctrinal standards.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith of the Evangelical United Brethren Church, Article IX (Justification and Regeneration)
further_reading.says: It says that although believers have experienced regeneration, it is possible to depart from grace and fall into sin, and that God's grace can renew them in righteousness.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Sermon 86, A Call to Backsliders
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that people who have fallen from justifying or sanctifying grace can be restored, and reads the hard passages of Hebrews as speaking of those who had known grace and renounced Christ.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article V (God's Purpose of Grace)
further_reading.says: It says that those whom God has accepted and sanctified will never fall away from the state of grace and are kept by God's power through faith.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 17 (Of the Perseverance of the Saints)
further_reading.says: It teaches that those God has accepted and sanctified cannot fall away totally or finally, that this rests on God's election and Christ's intercession, and that believers may fall into grievous sins and are then renewed to repentance.

further_reading.body: General Association of Regular Baptist Churches
further_reading.title: Articles of Faith, Article XIII (The Security of the Saints)
further_reading.says: It says that all who are truly born again are kept by God the Father for Jesus Christ, and cites Philippians 1:6, John 10:28-29, Romans 8:35-39 and Jude.

further_reading.body: National Association of Free Will Baptists
further_reading.title: Treatise of the Faith and Practices of the Free Will Baptists, chapter XIII (Perseverance of the Saints), 2026 edition
further_reading.says: It says that the truly regenerate are in danger of falling and are to watch and pray lest they be lost, and does not hold that a believer's final salvation is guaranteed.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (2017)
further_reading.says: The paper says the General Council disapproves of the unconditional security position (Bylaws, Article IX.B.1) and that salvation may be forfeited or abandoned by willfully turning away from Christ, while security rests on a continuing relationship with him.

further_reading.title: Dordrecht Confession of Faith (1632), Article XVI (Of the Ecclesiastical Ban)
further_reading.says: It describes the church's discipline of a member who sins again unto death and so becomes separated from God, forfeiting the kingdom of God, with the aim of amendment and not destruction.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 14 (Discipline in the Church)
further_reading.says: It describes church discipline as a sign of God's offer of forgiveness and transforming grace to believers who drift from faithful discipleship or fall into sin, aimed at restoring them to God and to the church.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 8 (Salvation), commentary
further_reading.says: It teaches that salvation is a gift of grace and that justification by faith and faithful obedience to the covenant are inseparable.

_why: QUOTES: each read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse?ref=... and ticked. Agreed: Eph 2:8 (full), John 6:37 (clause from 'the one who comes'), Matt 24:13 (clause), 1 Tim 4:1 (clause from 'in later times'). Reading 1: Heb 6:6 (full), Heb 10:26 (clause, trailing comma dropped), John 15:6 (full), Gal 5:4 (full), Rom 11:22 (the second sentence, from 'if you continue'), Col 1:23 (clause up to 'you heard'), 2 Pet 2:20 (full), Ezek 18:24 (from 'if a righteous man', through 'he will die'; the server's text begins 'But if'). Reading 2: John 10:28 (full), John 6:39 (clause), Rom 8:30 (full), Rom 8:39 (full), Phil 1:6 (clause from 'He who began'), 1 Pet 1:5 (full), 1 John 2:19 (first two sentences), Jer 32:40 (full). Reading 3: John 3:16 (full), John 5:24 (from 'whoever hears', through 'death to life'), Rom 8:1 (full), Eph 4:30 (full), 1 Cor 3:15 (full; the verse's own 'but only' is kept), 2 Tim 2:13 (clause), Heb 10:14 (full), 1 John 5:13 (full). All ticked; hyphens kept as the server has them (Heb 6:6). ORDER: by when each reading was articulated, as I read the history. First: falling away is possible, the reading of the early church and the churches that descend from it (Catholic, Orthodox), later restated by the Lutheran, Anabaptist and Wesleyan traditions. Second: the perseverance of the saints, stated in the Reformation churches from the 16th century and fixed in the Reformed confessions of the 17th. Third: eternal security in its popular form, which I place latest because I read it as the later restatement of the second reading without its account of election, in the Baptist and free-church line from about the 19th century; a reviewer who reads the history differently should say so. The order is by history and ranks nothing. THREE READINGS, 14, 14 and 13 PASSAGES after the 2026-10-26 verse audit (eight each before it), each added verse cited by several of the sources read for its reading. WARNING AND ASSURANCE PASSAGES: Hebrews 6 and 10 are quoted in reading 1 (Heb 6:6, Heb 10:26) and answered in readings 2 and 3 (Heb 6:4-6, 6:9, 10:26-29, 10:39, 3:14), John 10 appears in reading 2 (John 10:28) and is answered in reading 1 (John 10:27-29) and Romans 8 appears in reading 2 (8:30, 8:39) and is answered in reading 1 (8:38-39) and Rom 8:1 in reading 3. Each reading's way of reading the other's verses is in its 'answers'. HELD_BY: assignments are approximate. The summaries say where a tradition differs within itself: Anglican (in readings 1 and 2), Lutheran (in 1: the tradition holds that a believer can fall and that God keeps believers in faith; Lutherans also speak of assurance in the promise, which I did not state because it would read as favouring the second reading), Baptist (2 and 3), Pentecostal (1 and 3), Wesleyan (1). The Reformed are credited only with reading 2. Nothing names a person, scholar or leader. WORDS: summaries, answers and notes checked for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely': none appear in my own wording. 'But' and 'only' appear inside the quotes where the Berean has them (1 Cor 3:15 'but only', 2 Pet 2:20 'only to be', John 3:16 'but have'). 'Not ... and not' contrasts that describe what a tradition says appear in the summaries and answers; they state the tradition's own distinction and are not a verdict. THE HARD CALLS: (a) Reading 1 groups seven traditions whose accounts differ (mortal sin, free turning, falling from grace, falling from faith); I named the differences in the summary and left them in one reading because the card asks the one question; a Lutheran reviewer may want the Lutheran account of being kept in faith given its own sentence or a separate reading, and a Catholic or Orthodox reviewer may want a lighter hand on the Wesleyan 'can return'. (b) Reading 3 is a smaller family within reading 2's neighbours; its summary says its holders differ on whether every believer keeps believing, and that some take the warnings as reading 2 does. (c) Ezekiel 18:24 in reading 1 is the one Old Testament verse; a rabbi should say whether the card handles it fairly: reading 1 takes it as a pattern the New Testament warnings continue, reading 2 as life in Israel's covenant. The Jewish teaching on repentance and a righteous man's turning is not stated and probably should be in some way (as it is in the verse). (d) Reading 2's phrase 'people whose faith was not the saving kind' is the holders' way of putting it; a reader attentive to the wider church may find it sharp, and the summary says it is theirs. LEFT OUT (after the 2026-10-26 verse audit, which added Heb 3:12, Heb 10:38, 1 Cor 9:27 and 10:12, 1 Tim 1:19, Luke 8:13, Eph 1:13 and 4:30, Heb 7:25, John 17:11, Luke 22:32 and Jude 24 as passages): Rev 3:5 (cited by both sides: 'never blot out' and the implication that names might be), Heb 3:14, Heb 6:4-5 (quoted inside notes only), Heb 10:29, Heb 10:39 (quoted in reading 2's answers, not as a passage), Heb 12:15, 2 Tim 2:12, John 17:12 (Judas, cited by both sides), Matt 7:22-23 ('I never knew you', cited in reading 2), Rom 11:29, 2 Cor 1:22, 1 Cor 1:8-9, 1 Thess 5:23-24. These are all citable; a reviewer may want one added where it belongs. RELATED: themes are deliverance, judgment, covenant, mercy_restoration and spirit, all ids in /api/majorthemes. Cards are salvation, faith, grace, endurance, eternal_life, abide, justification and covenant, each confirmed with /api/entity?id=. I did not list the sibling cards (free-will, election, human-nature, total-depravity) because they may not exist yet; the owner can add them when they do. 'Perseverance', 'apostasy' and 'assurance' have no entity of their own. UNRESOLVED: whether 'Pentecostal / Charismatic' belongs in reading 3 as well as 1 (stated as 'some churches'); how the Lutheran account is best stated; the order in readings 2 and 3 (history is arguable).
